dossiers.morale-marches.hook: A fine for late parents that makes them… arrive even later. A compensation that makes people refuse a project they accepted for free. A right to pollute bought on the stock market. A kidney you can legally sell in Iran. How far should the market go? A long course for thinking, with real facts and experiments.
dossiers.morale-marches.tldr.0: Economists first judge a market by its efficiency; Harvard philosopher Michael Sandel asks two other questions: is it fair (fairness), and does money change the nature of what is being exchanged (corruption)?
dossiers.morale-marches.tldr.1: Real experiments show that a price can drive out moral motivation: in Israeli daycare centers, a fine increased lateness [1]; in Switzerland, offering compensation made acceptance of a nuclear waste site drop from about half to about a quarter of residents [10][11].
dossiers.morale-marches.tldr.2: But a price can also be accepted and effective: the European carbon market has accompanied a drop of about 50% in emissions from the covered sectors since 2005 [13], and Stockholm's congestion charge, unpopular at first, was adopted by referendum after a trial [14].
dossiers.morale-marches.tldr.3: Paying students, paying for blood, selling a kidney: incentives work… sometimes, and not always as planned [5][9][6]. Some markets are also rejected because they shock people, what economist Alvin Roth calls “repugnance” [12].
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.0.title: The question we no longer ask
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.0.parag: Since the 1980s, the market has expanded into areas that used to be beyond its reach: health, education, the environment, security, privacy. For an economist, a freely agreed exchange benefits both parties; if a market can be created where there was none, efficiency often improves, meaning we get more from the same resources.

Harvard philosopher Michael Sandel, known for his “Justice” course taken by thousands of students, sums up his worry in one phrase: we have moved ==from a market economy to a market society==. A market economy is a tool for producing goods. A market society is a way of life where almost everything is for sale.

He raises two objections. ==Fairness==: is an exchange really free when one of the two parties is in need? ==Corruption==, in the sense of “degradation”: putting a price on certain things changes what they are; a bought Nobel Prize is no longer a Nobel Prize, a bought friendship is no longer a friendship.

This course does not settle the matter: it gives you real cases, with their figures, so that you can form your own opinion. You will see that money sometimes has exactly the intended effect, sometimes the opposite effect, and that the line between what “can be sold” and what “cannot be sold” varies across countries and eras.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.1.title: Everything is for sale? Some real prices
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.1.parag: Sandel's book “What Money Can't Buy” (2012) opens with a list of very real prices. In California, ==an inmate can pay about $82 a night for a cleaner, quieter cell== [8]. In Dallas schools, young students were paid ==$2 per book read== to encourage them to read [8]. And in Washington, you can pay someone to stand in line for you ahead of a congressional hearing [8].
For the economist, nothing shocking: everyone gets what they want, the inmate better sleep, the prison revenue, the lobbyist a seat, the “line stander” an income. Both sides win, no one is forced.

For Sandel, each example raises one of his two questions. The paid cell: is it fair that comfort in prison depends on the inmate's money? The $2 per book: does the child learn to love reading, or to read for money? The line: should a public hearing be more accessible to lobbyists who pay than to citizens who wait?

==These examples are not isolated abuses==, says Sandel: they show a trend. The more money matters for access to the good things in life (health, education, security, political influence), the more income inequality weighs on everyone's life.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.2.title: The two objections, up close
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.2.parag: ==Fairness, or coercion.== An exchange is only truly free if each side can say no without losing much. When someone sells a kidney to pay off a debt, or accepts a dangerous job because they have nothing else, we may wonder whether they are really choosing. This objection does not target the market itself: it targets the inequalities that distort it. In a more equal society, it would lose some of its force.

==Corruption, or degradation.== This objection runs deeper: even between two equally rich people, putting a price on something can change its meaning. Donated blood becomes sold blood, civic service becomes a job, reading becomes paid work. Here, inequality is not the problem; money itself is.

Economists often answer that money does not change things: a book read is a book read, whatever the reason. But a branch of economics, behavioral economics, has shown that they are sometimes wrong. It speaks of ==the crowding-out of motivation==: a cash reward can drive out a deeper motivation (duty, pride, the desire to help), and in the end, people do less.
The following sections present the best-known experiments on this subject. Keep this framework in mind: for each case, ask yourself ==whether the price works, and what it changes==.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.3.title: The fine that made parents come… later
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.3.parag: Economists Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini ran an experiment in daycare centers in Israel. For four weeks, they simply counted parents' late arrivals. Then, in 6 of 10 centers, they introduced a fine for parents arriving more than 10 minutes late; the other 4 served as a comparison [1].

The result was the opposite of what was expected: ==lateness increased== in the centers with a fine, then stabilized at a higher level than before. And when the fine was removed, in week 17, lateness stayed just as high [1]. In the centers without a fine, nothing changed.

Their explanation is in the title of their paper: ==“a fine is a price”==. Before, being late meant disrespecting the caregivers who were waiting. With the fine, it became a service you pay for: the moral discomfort disappeared. And it did not come back when the fine was withdrawn [1].

A lesson for any public policy: ==a social norm, once replaced by a price, does not necessarily return when the price is removed==. The authors also note that the fine was small; a much heavier fine would probably have reduced lateness. The problem is not money in general, it is a small price replacing a moral obligation.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.3.plain: how a price kills a norm
Before: a late parent feels guilty toward the caregiver who is waiting. They do everything to arrive on time.
The daycare creates a fine for lateness of more than 10 minutes [1].
The parent thinks: “I pay, so I'm entitled.” Lateness becomes a purchased service.
Lateness increases. Even when the fine disappears, the guilt does not return: lateness stays high [1].
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.4.title: When money drives out civic spirit: Swiss nuclear waste
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.4.parag: In the early 1990s, Switzerland was looking for a place to store its low- and medium-level radioactive nuclear waste. Economists Bruno Frey and Felix Oberholzer-Gee took the opportunity to survey residents [10][11].

First question: would you accept the site in your municipality? ==About half of the residents surveyed said yes== (50.8% according to the survey), despite the perceived risk [11]. Many saw it as a civic duty: this waste has to be stored somewhere.

Second question: and if the country paid you a substantial compensation every year? Logically, acceptance should rise, since a benefit is being added. ==It collapses to about a quarter== (24.6%) [11]. The authors explain it with two effects: the money is seen as a bribe, and it replaces the sense of duty with a calculation in which the risk then seems too poorly paid [10].

This experiment is often cited by Sandel: ==adding a price does not always add to moral motivation; it can replace it==. It does not mean that residents near an unwelcome facility should never be compensated. It says that the way of compensating matters: a check to each resident does not mean the same as a project for the whole municipality.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.4.plain: why a check can make people say no
We ask: “Would you accept this site for the good of the country?” One resident in two says yes, out of duty [11].
We add: “You will be paid every year.” The question changes in nature.
The resident thinks: “If they're paying me, it must be dangerous, and is this price enough?” Duty fades, calculation begins.
Only one resident in four still says yes [11]: compensation drove out civic spirit [10].
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.5.title: Paying for blood?
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.5.parag: In 1970, British sociologist Richard Titmuss compared, in “The Gift Relationship,” free blood donation in the United Kingdom with paid blood in the United States. He defended an idea that at first made economists smile: ==paying for blood could reduce the number of donors== and the quality of the blood, because money would drive out the spirit of giving [9].

Nearly forty years later, in 2008, Swedish economists Carl Mellström and Magnus Johannesson tested this idea in Gothenburg. People interested in donating blood were randomly split into three groups: no payment, 50 kronor (about $7), or the choice between those 50 kronor and a donation of the same amount to a charity [9].

Among men, payment changes nothing. Among women, ==the share of volunteers falls from about 52% to 30% when they are paid== [9]. And when they can donate the money to a charity, the share goes back up to the level of the no-payment group [9]. The authors offer an explanation: donating blood is also a way of showing that you are generous, and payment blurs that signal [9].

Titmuss was therefore partly right, but not for everyone. Today, most European countries, including France, rely on voluntary unpaid blood donation; others, like the United States, pay for plasma donation. ==The same product, two philosophies.==
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.6.title: Pay to pollute?
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.6.parag: Since 2005, the European Union has required power plants, factories and airlines to hold an “allowance” for each tonne of CO₂ they emit. The total number of allowances is capped and falls over time; companies can buy and resell them [2].

The price moves like a market. Around 4 euros a tonne in February 2017, it exceeds ==100 euros for the first time in February 2023== [2], before falling back below 60 euros in 2024 [3]. According to the European Commission, ==emissions from the covered sectors have fallen by about 50% since 2005==, mainly thanks to electricity generation [13].

For economists, it is the most efficient tool: the quantity of pollution is fixed, and the companies that cut at the lowest cost cut the most. For Sandel, the phrase “right to pollute” is a problem: ==paying to pollute strips pollution of its character as a wrong==, just as the daycare fine stripped lateness of its character as impoliteness. He gives the example of the difference between a fine (a penalty) and a price (a service): an allowance looks like a price.

France also has a carbon tax on fuels and heating. It reached 44.6 euros a tonne in 2018; the increase planned for 2019 was cancelled after the yellow vests movement, and it has stayed frozen at that level ever since, far from the 100 euros targeted for 2030 [4]. ==A price that is efficient on paper can be judged unfair in the street==, especially by those who have no choice but to use a car.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.6.plain: Europe sets a total cap on emissions and distributes or sells allowances: 1 allowance = 1 tonne of CO₂ [2].
A factory that can cut its emissions cheaply does so, and resells its surplus allowances.
A factory for which it is very expensive buys allowances rather than cutting.

In total, emissions respect the cap, at the lowest possible cost. The cap falls each year: the allowance price rises, and polluting costs more and more [2]. Result: about 50% fewer emissions in these sectors since 2005 [13].
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.7.title: Paying to drive: London and Stockholm
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.7.parag: A congestion charge is another “price” put on a behavior: driving in the city center at rush hour. In ==February 2003, London introduced a charge of 5 pounds a day== to enter the center on weekdays, from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. [14]. Traffic fell markedly from the launch, and support among Londoners grew in the following months [14].

Stockholm chose an original method: ==a seven-month trial, from January to July 2006, followed by a referendum== in September 2006 [14]. Before the trial, the charge was very unpopular. After seeing it work (fewer traffic jams, faster buses), 53% of voters approved it, and it became permanent in 2007 [14].

This example shows the other side of the debate: ==a price can be accepted when people see its effects and when the money is used for something visible==, such as public transport. Here, the price does not destroy a moral norm; it replaces the queue of traffic jams, where everyone wastes time, with a fee.

Sandel himself does not reject all prices. His question is always: what value does this good have, and does the price respect it? Driving in a city center is not a moral act; traffic there is a scarce good that must be shared, and a price can do so more fairly than congestion.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.8.title: Pay students to learn?
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.8.parag: In 2007-2009, Harvard economist Roland Fryer tested cash incentives in more than 250 schools in Chicago, Dallas, Washington and New York, with randomly assigned groups [5]. In Dallas, students were paid to read books; elsewhere, for their grades.

Result: ==paying for outcomes (grades) does not work==, whereas paying for effort (reading, coming to class, behaving well) has more encouraging effects [5]. Fryer's explanation: students want the reward, but do not know how to turn their desire into better grades; paying for a concrete action they can control works better [5].

Sandel replies with another question: even if the incentives worked, ==what does the child learn?== That you read to earn money, or that you read because it is fascinating? If the reading habit disappears when the incentive stops, just as lateness stayed high after the daycare fine, the gain is fragile.
The lesson echoes that of the daycare centers and Swiss waste: ==a price changes behavior, but not always in the intended direction, and sometimes it also changes the reasons why we act==.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.9.title: Can you sell a kidney?
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.9.parag: Almost everywhere, selling an organ is prohibited. Iran is an exception: since 1988, a state-regulated program has allowed an unrelated living donor to receive money for a kidney [6].

Its defenders claim it eliminated the waiting list for a kidney transplant in the late 1990s; this claim is disputed by other Iranian specialists, who point to the poverty of donors and to how the waiting list is measured [6][7].

It is the perfect case for Sandel's two objections: ==is the donor really free== if they sell a kidney because they are poor (fairness)? And does a gift turned into a sale keep the same meaning (corruption)? On the other side, the economic argument: thousands of patients elsewhere wait for a transplant, and some die before receiving one.

Economist Alvin Roth, 2012 Nobel laureate, found a third way: ==kidney exchanges without money==. When a loved one wants to give a kidney to a patient but is not compatible, an exchange is arranged with another pair in the same situation: each donor gives to the other's patient. Roth helped create the New England kidney exchange program in the United States [12]. These exchanges do not provoke the rejection that payment for organs does [12].
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.9.plain: Paul wants to give a kidney to his wife Anne, but they are not compatible.
In another city, Léa wants to give a kidney to her brother Marc: not compatible either.
By luck, Paul is compatible with Marc, and Léa with Anne.
The exchange is arranged: Paul gives to Marc, Léa gives to Anne. Two transplants, no payment, and no one sold their body: this is the principle of the exchanges Roth helped organize [12].
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.10.para: In 2007, Alvin Roth published a paper with a telling title: ==“Repugnance as a Constraint on Markets”== [12]. He starts from a simple example: in California, a law prohibits serving horse meat in restaurants, even though California is a very diverse state where many cultures eat it [12].

Roth observes that some exchanges are prohibited not because they harm anyone, but because many people find them repugnant. And this feeling ==often targets the money, not the exchange itself==: giving a kidney is admired, swapping it for another kidney is accepted, selling it is prohibited almost everywhere [12].

Repugnance changes over time and across countries. Lending money at interest was long condemned by the Church; life insurance first shocked, because it put a price on death; today, they are commonplace. Conversely, practices that were once common have become unacceptable.

For Roth, the economist must take repugnance seriously as a given, and look for solutions that respect it (like kidney exchanges). For Sandel, ==repugnance is not just a feeling to work around: it often signals a real value== that must be openly discussed.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.11.para: ==The efficiency camp== asks: does the market produce the best outcome at the lowest cost? It points out that bans also have victims (patients without transplants, unpriced pollution, traffic jams) and that a well-designed price can achieve a shared goal, like the drop in European emissions [13].

==Sandel's camp== asks: which values does the price make disappear, and who is forced to accept the exchange? It points out that a society where everything is for sale becomes harsher for those who have little, and that experiments show money can drive out civic spirit [1][10][11].

The two camps are not always opposed. Stockholm's congestion charge [14] or kidney exchanges [12] show that an arrangement that is both efficient and accepted can sometimes be found. And the daycare fine shows that an economist attentive to social norms could have predicted the failure [1].

In public debate, these two camps meet constantly: carbon tax, congestion charges, water prices, payment for blood or plasma donation, student incentives, surrogate mothers, university admission fees. ==Being able to recognize the question being asked (efficiency or values?) helps you understand the disagreement==, and often makes it less bitter.
dossiers.morale-marches.sections.11.exam: For each case, ask the three questions: 1) Is it efficient? 2) Is the exchange really free, or is one side coerced? 3) Does the price change the meaning of the thing? Daycare fine, Swiss compensation, paid blood, CO₂ allowance, congestion charge, school incentive, paid kidney, kidney exchange: you will see that the answers do not always point in the same direction.
dossiers.morale-marches.forMe: Whenever someone proposes to “put a price” on something (polluting, parking, going first, passing an exam, donating blood), ask yourself whether it is about making the system more efficient, or whether the price changes how people behave and judge their actions. And look at how the money is used: a price whose usefulness is visible is far better accepted.

dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.0.q: What happened to lateness in the daycare centers where a fine was introduced?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.0.explain: The fine turned lateness into a paid service: lateness increased and stayed high even after the fine was removed.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.1.q: What difference does Sandel draw between a “market economy” and a “market society”?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.1.options.1: One is a tool for producing, the other a way of life where almost everything is for sale
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.1.options.2: One is French, the other American
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.1.options.3: One has a stock exchange, the other does not
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.1.explain: Sandel is worried about the shift from one to the other since the 1980s.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.2.q: What are Sandel's two objections to markets?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.2.options.1: Fairness and corruption (the price changes the meaning of the thing)
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.2.explain: Fairness: an exchange under coercion is not truly free. Corruption: putting a price on certain things degrades them.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.3.q: In Switzerland, what did offering residents compensation for hosting nuclear waste cause?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.3.options.1: Acceptance dropped from about half to about a quarter
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.3.explain: The compensation was seen as a bribe and replaced the sense of duty with a calculation: this is the crowding-out effect.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.4.q: In the Swedish blood donation experiment, who was discouraged by payment?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.4.explain: Among women, the share of volunteers fell from about 52% to 30%; among men, there was no effect.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.5.q: How does the European carbon market work?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.5.options.1: An emissions cap and allowances that are bought and resold
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.5.explain: One allowance per tonne of CO₂, a falling total cap, and companies trading their allowances; about −50% emissions since 2005 in these sectors.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.6.q: How did Stockholm get its congestion charge accepted?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.6.options.0: By imposing it without a vote
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.6.options.1: Through a seven-month trial followed by a referendum
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.6.explain: After seeing its effects in 2006, 53% of voters approved it; it has been permanent since 2007.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.7.q: In Fryer's experiment, what works least well?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.7.explain: Paying for outcomes does not work: students do not know how to turn the reward into better grades.
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.8.q: What non-monetary solution did Alvin Roth help organize for transplants?
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.8.options.1: Kidney exchanges between incompatible donor-patient pairs
dossiers.morale-marches.quiz.8.explain: Each donor gives to the other pair's patient: two transplants, no payment.
